blocks.prompt: The Seed That Will Not Listen
blocks.text: Cut an apple across the middle, not up and down. Inside you will find a star with five points. A seed sits in each point. Here is the strange part. If you plant one of those seeds, it will not grow your apple. It grows a different apple. It might be sour. It might be tiny and hard. Nobody knows until the tree makes fruit, and that takes years of waiting. So how do farmers get the same apple again and again? They do not use seeds. They cut a small twig from a tree they like. They join the twig onto another young tree and wrap it up tight. The twig grows, and it makes the very same apple as the tree it came from.

blocks.prompt: One Tree, Everywhere
blocks.text: An apple tree does not make copies of itself. Every seed inside an apple carries a brand new mix: a little from the tree it grew on, and a little from the tree whose pollen a bee carried over. Plant that seed and you get a tree nobody has ever tasted. Most of them make small, sour fruit. That is why growers do not plant seeds. Instead they graft. A grower cuts a twig from a tree that makes good apples, joins it to the trunk of a young rooted tree, and wraps the joint tight. The two grow together into one tree, and the twig keeps making the apples it always made. This leads somewhere surprising. Every Granny Smith apple in the world came from one tree. In Australia, around 1868, a woman named Maria Ann Smith found a seedling growing near her creek, where she had tossed out the scraps of some sour cooking apples. The fruit on it was green, hard, and tart, and people liked it. Growers cut twigs from her tree and grafted them. Then they cut twigs from those trees, and on and on, for over a hundred and fifty years. Every Granny Smith you have ever eaten is a piece of Maria Smith's tree.

blocks.prompt: The Forest Where Apples Are Wild
blocks.text: Ask where apples come from and the honest answer is a mountain range you have probably never heard of. In the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan there are forests where the trees are apple trees. Not orchards. Wild forest, growing apples on its own, long before anyone planted anything. The species is called Malus sieversii, and it is the ancestor of nearly every apple in your grocery store. Kazakhstan's largest city, Almaty, sits right at the edge of those forests, and its name comes from the word for apple. Bears eat the wild fruit. So do horses and deer. The seeds ride through the animals and get dropped somewhere new, and because every apple seed is a fresh mix, every dropped seed becomes a slightly different tree. The forest is a machine for making variety. Most of those trees make bitter little marbles. A few make fruit as good as anything in a supermarket. Traders on the Silk Road tasted their way through, picked the good ones, and carried them west into Persia, Greece, Rome, and eventually all of Europe. Americans usually meet apples through Johnny Appleseed. He was a real person. John Chapman walked the Ohio frontier in the early 1800s planting apple nurseries, and he really did wear rough clothes and sleep outdoors. But he planted seeds, not grafts, and seedling apples are mostly hard and sour. Almost none of his trees made good eating fruit. That was not a mistake. Those apples were meant to be pressed into cider, which kept far longer than fresh fruit and sat on nearly every frontier table. The Johnny Appleseed of the storybooks hands out sweet snacks. The real one was planting a drink.

notes: A picked apple is still alive and breathing
Ethylene is the gas that says ripen now
Controlled atmosphere storage holds apples for a year
Browning is an enzyme meeting oxygen
Lemon juice slows the browning down
About a quarter of an apple's volume is air

blocks.prompt: The Apple in Your Lunch Might Be a Year Old
blocks.text: Pick an apple in October and eat it the following June. By rights it should be a soft brown lump. Instead it snaps when you bite it. That is not luck. It is chemistry, and people spent a century working it out. Start with why apples go bad at all. A picked apple is still alive. It keeps breathing, taking in oxygen and burning through its own stored sugars, and the faster it breathes the faster it collapses into mush. It also releases a gas called ethylene, the signal fruit uses to tell itself, and everything sitting near it, to get on with ripening. Ethylene is why one rotting apple really can ruin a whole barrel. The bad apple is not spreading rot from fruit to fruit. It is shouting a command, and the other apples obey. In the 1920s two British scientists, Franklin Kidd and Cyril West, asked a blunt question. If the apple is breathing, what happens if we take most of its air away? They sealed apples into cold rooms, pulled the oxygen down to around one or two percent, roughly a twentieth of what is in the room you are sitting in, and let carbon dioxide build up. The apples did not suffocate. They idled. Breathing slowed to a crawl, ethylene barely moved, and fruit that should have failed in weeks came out firm many months later. The method is called controlled atmosphere storage, and almost every apple you buy outside of autumn has been asleep in one. The rooms hold so little oxygen that a worker who walked in without an air supply would pass out. Browning is a separate problem with a separate answer. Cut an apple and the knife tears open cells, which lets an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase meet the oxygen in the air. The two react within minutes and the pale flesh goes rust brown. The apple is not dirty and it is not spoiled. It is bruising, in the same way you do. Squeeze lemon juice over the slices and the browning stalls, because the acid and the vitamin C in the juice jam the enzyme before it can get started. None of this makes the apple better than it was. It makes it patient. The fruit is doing exactly what it has always done. We have simply learned how to talk it into waiting.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Malus domestica, from wild Malus sieversii
A pome: most of the flesh is not the ovary
Self-incompatible: it needs another tree's pollen
Extremely heterozygous, so seedlings never match
Every named variety is a graft, meaning a clone
Honeycrisp was released in 1991 by Minnesota breeders

blocks.prompt: Every Apple Is a Clone, and That Is the Problem
blocks.text: Start with an inconvenient fact about the apple in your hand. Botanically, most of it is not fruit. A fruit, in the strict sense, develops from the ovary of a flower. In an apple, the ovary becomes the papery core, those five little chambers holding the seeds. The part you actually eat swelled out of the base of the flower itself, the tissue that once carried the petals. Botanists call the result a pome, an accessory fruit. The apple built a snack around its seeds out of spare parts, because a fruit is not a gift. It is a bribe. An animal eats the sweet tissue, walks off, and deposits the seeds somewhere else along with a supply of fertilizer. That bribe only pays if the seeds are worth moving, and here the apple makes a choice that looks reckless. Apple trees are self-incompatible, which means a tree's own pollen will not fertilize its own flowers. Every apple requires pollen carried, usually by a bee, from a genetically different tree. On top of that, apples are extremely heterozygous: the two copies of each gene in a tree are unusually different from one another. Shuffle two such genomes together and the offspring come out wildly unlike either parent. Plant a seed from a Honeycrisp and you do not get a Honeycrisp. You get a stranger. Most strangers are disappointing, and plenty are bitter enough to make your jaw ache. So the apple hands growers a paradox. The trait that makes the species brilliant, relentless variation, makes it useless as a crop. Humans solved that with a knife. Cut a twig from a tree whose fruit you like, join it to a rooted stump, seal the wound, and the twig goes on growing as itself. The tree that results is not a descendant. It is the same individual, continued. Every Granny Smith traces back to one seedling found in Australia around 1868. Every Red Delicious traces to a single chance tree on Jesse Hiatt's farm in Iowa, which he cut down and which grew back, twice, until he gave up and tasted it. When you eat those varieties you are eating a tree that has been alive, in pieces, for well over a century. The convenience carries a cost. A clone cannot adapt. Every tree of a variety meets a new fungus or a new beetle with identical defenses, which is to say with identical weaknesses, and an orchard of identical trees is an open invitation to anything that can crack one of them. Growers answer with sprays, and the pest answers back, and the cycle has no end in it. Meanwhile the trees that might supply new defenses, or new flavors, grow mostly in the wild apple forests of the Tian Shan in Kazakhstan, where Malus sieversii still stands on its own and no two trees are alike. Those forests are being cleared for housing and grazing. Researchers now collect cuttings from them the way librarians rescue books from a burning building. Occasionally the shuffle is worth the wait. Honeycrisp came out of a breeding program at the University of Minnesota and was released in 1991, after decades of crossing and culling seedlings nobody wanted. Its cells are unusually large, and when you bite down they rupture instead of tearing apart from each other, which floods your mouth with juice and makes the snap the variety is famous for. Every Honeycrisp on Earth is a graft of that one seedling. Which leaves the apple in a strange position. It is among the most thoroughly domesticated plants we have. We control where it grows, how tall it gets, and how long it keeps. And yet we have never once persuaded it to reproduce the way we want. We cannot breed a Honeycrisp. We can only copy the one we happened to find.
